specPoints.text: describe the effects on the atomic and mass numbers of a nucleus of the emission of each of the four main types of radiation (alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation)
understand how to balance nuclear equations in terms of mass and charge

primer.text: Every emission rewrites the nucleus in a predictable way: alpha removes two protons and two neutrons, beta promotes a neutron to a proton, gamma changes nothing but energy, and neutron emission trims one nucleon. Balance mass and charge either side and any decay equation yields.

lessons.title: Alpha and beta decay
lessons.opening: In alpha decay the nucleus ejects a helium nucleus, cutting its mass number by 4 and its atomic number by 2 — a new element forms. In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton and an emitted electron, so the mass number holds while the atomic number rises by 1.
keyPoints: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, so the daughter element is a different element.
Beta decay changes a neutron into a proton plus an emitted electron.
In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number increases by 1.
A beta particle has mass number 0 and atomic number −1 in nuclear notation.

low.restatement: Alpha: subtract 4 from the top number and 2 from the bottom. Beta: top number stays, bottom number climbs by 1.
low.analogy: Alpha is throwing a four-person lifeboat off a ship (two oarsmen, two passengers gone); beta is a crew member switching uniforms but staying aboard.
low.examPointer: Write the two number changes per emission as a mini-table — examiners award the arithmetic even if element names are unknown.

medium.restatement: The emitted alpha carries A = 4, Z = 2, so nucleon and proton conservation fix the daughter. In beta decay charge conservation requires Z to rise by 1 because the emitted electron carries charge −1 while the nucleon total stays constant.
medium.analogy: The nuclear ledger never lies: whatever leaves the nucleus is deducted from its accounts, and both the mass and the charge columns must still balance.
medium.examPointer: Element names are never required — only the balanced numbers. Do not waste time memorising daughters.

check.stem: What happens to the mass number of a nucleus that emits an alpha particle?

options.explanation: The alpha removes two protons and two neutrons.
Two is the atomic-number change.
Beta leaves the mass number; alpha does not.
Emission removes, never adds, nucleons.

check.stem: In beta decay, the atomic number of the daughter nucleus…

options.explanation: The neutron-to-proton conversion adds one proton.
That would need a proton-to-neutron change.
Gamma or neutron emission leaves Z; beta does not.
Nothing in beta decay scales by two.

check.stem: A beta particle is best described as…

options.text: an electron emitted from the nucleus
options.explanation: Beta-minus is a nuclear electron.
That is alpha.
That is gamma.
Neutron emission is a separate mode.

check.stem: Why does a nucleus that emits an alpha particle become a different element?

options.text: because its atomic number falls by 2, and the proton count defines the element
options.explanation: Identity follows the proton count.
Mass change alone would leave the element (an isotope).
Electrons are irrelevant to element identity.
The identity change is arithmetic, not a label.

check.stem: Which emission leaves both the mass number and the atomic number unchanged?

options.explanation: Gamma carries energy but no nucleons or charge.
Alpha changes both numbers.
Beta changes the atomic number.
It lowers the mass number by 1.

check.stem: State the changes in mass number and atomic number when a nucleus emits an alpha particle.
check.modelAnswer: The mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2.

check.stem: Describe what happens to a neutron during beta decay.
check.modelAnswer: The neutron changes into a proton, which stays in the nucleus, and an electron, which is emitted as the beta particle.

check.stem: Explain why the mass number is unchanged in beta decay but the atomic number rises by 1.
check.modelAnswer: A neutron becomes a proton: the total nucleon count is unchanged, so the mass number stays; the proton count rises by one, so the atomic number increases by 1.

check.stem: A nucleus of atomic number 88 and mass number 226 emits an alpha particle. State the atomic and mass numbers of the daughter nucleus.
check.modelAnswer: Alpha decay: atomic number 88 − 2 = 86, mass number 226 − 4 = 222.

lessons.title: Gamma decay and neutron emission
lessons.opening: Gamma decay lets an excited nucleus shed pure energy: no protons or neutrons leave, so both numbers stay the same. Neutron emission instead trims one nucleon — the mass number falls by 1 while the atomic number holds, producing another isotope of the same element.
keyPoints: Gamma emission carries away energy but no mass or charge.
After gamma decay the mass and atomic numbers are exactly as before.
Neutron emission lowers the mass number by 1 and leaves the atomic number unchanged.
Neutron emission turns a nucleus into another isotope of the same element.

low.restatement: Gamma: same element, same numbers, less energy. Neutron emission: top number down by 1, bottom number unchanged — same element, lighter isotope.
low.analogy: Gamma is a hot pan cooling without losing any ingredients; neutron emission is tipping one marble out of a jar — same marbles, one fewer.
low.examPointer: Neutron emission is the odd one out: know its A − 1, Z rule alongside the other three.

medium.restatement: Because gamma carries neither nucleon number nor charge, conservation leaves the nucleus identity and both counts intact — only its energy state drops. Neutron emission removes a neutral nucleon, so charge is conserved trivially and the proton count, hence the element, is fixed.
medium.analogy: Gamma decay is venting steam from a kettle (nothing material leaves); neutron emission is dropping one coin from a purse of mixed coins — the denominations (elements) are unchanged, the total (mass) falls.
medium.examPointer: Isotope questions: "same element, different mass" points to neutron emission as the decay route.

check.stem: What does a gamma ray carry away from a nucleus?

options.explanation: Gamma has no mass and no charge — pure energy.
That is alpha’s cargo.
That is neutron emission.
That is beta’s cargo.

check.stem: After neutron emission, the daughter nucleus is…

options.text: another isotope of the same element
options.explanation: Proton count unchanged, mass number down by one.
The atomic number did not change.
The mass number fell by 1.
Nothing helium-like is involved.

check.stem: How do the mass and atomic numbers change in gamma decay?

options.explanation: Gamma changes neither count.
That is neutron emission.
That is alpha decay.
That is beta decay.

check.stem: A nucleus emits a neutron. Its new mass number is…

options.explanation: One nucleon left the nucleus.
Emission reduces the count.
Four is the alpha loss.
Only gamma leaves the mass number alone.

check.stem: Why does neutron emission not change the chemical identity of the atom?

options.text: because the proton count, which defines the element, is untouched
options.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge and no proton number.
Protons decide the element.

options.text: because the emitted neutron takes a proton with it
options.explanation: It leaves alone.
The electron count is not what identity rests on.

check.stem: State the effect of gamma emission on the mass number and atomic number.
check.modelAnswer: Both the mass number and the atomic number remain the same, because gamma carries no protons, neutrons or charge.

check.stem: State the changes caused by neutron emission.
check.modelAnswer: The mass number decreases by 1 and the atomic number stays the same, forming another isotope of the same element.

check.stem: Explain why gamma decay can leave a nucleus with identical numbers yet a different state.
check.modelAnswer: Gamma carries only energy, so no protons or neutrons leave; the nucleus keeps its composition but loses surplus energy, settling into a lower-energy state.

check.stem: A nucleus has mass number 9 and atomic number 4 and emits a neutron. Give the daughter’s numbers and say what relation it bears to the original.
check.modelAnswer: The daughter has mass number 9 − 1 = 8 and atomic number 4; with the same proton count it is another isotope of the same element.

lessons.title: Balancing nuclear equations
lessons.opening: A decay equation must balance in both mass number and atomic number: the totals before the arrow equal the totals after. Check any equation by adding top numbers and bottom numbers separately — polonium-212 decaying to lead-208 plus an alpha is the model case.
keyPoints: Particles before the decay sit before the arrow; products sit after it.
The sum of mass numbers is equal on both sides of a balanced equation.
The sum of atomic numbers is equal on both sides as well.
You never need the daughter’s element name — only its balanced numbers.

low.restatement: Add the top numbers each side; they must match. Add the bottom numbers each side; they must match. If either pair differs, the equation is wrong.
low.analogy: It is a till receipt: whatever leaves the till (nucleus) must appear itemised on the customer’s side.
low.examPointer: Show both checks explicitly (mass, then charge) — the working is worth as much as the answer.

medium.restatement: Conservation of nucleon number and of charge underwrites the two balances. Unknown daughters are solved algebraically: write A, Z for the missing particle and equate sums, which recovers alpha (4, 2), beta (0, −1), gamma (0, 0) or neutron (1, 0) emissions from the arithmetic alone.
medium.analogy: Two accounting columns that must reconcile — the missing entry is whatever makes the columns add up.
medium.examPointer: For "find the missing particle" questions, compute ΔA and ΔZ first; the pair (4,2), (0,−1), (0,0), (1,0) names the emission.

check.stem: In the decay of polonium-212 (Z = 84) to lead-208 plus alpha, which balance holds?

options.explanation: Both the mass and the atomic columns balance exactly.
The 4 belongs with mass, the 2 with atomic number.
The atomic balance needs 2, the alpha’s protons.
The daughter mass is 208, not 206.

check.stem: A decay equation for beta emission must show the beta particle with…

options.explanation: The electron carries charge −1 and negligible mass.
Those are alpha’s numbers.
Those are a neutron’s numbers.
A positive electron is not beta-minus.

check.stem: An unknown emission leaves ΔA = 0 and ΔZ = 0 for the nucleus. The missing particle is…

options.explanation: Zero mass and zero charge change is gamma.
Alpha gives ΔA = 4, ΔZ = 2.
Beta gives ΔZ = 1.
Neutron emission gives ΔA = 1.

check.stem: The nucleus with atomic number 11 and mass number 24 undergoes beta decay. The daughter has…

options.explanation: Z rises to 12; A stays at 24.
Beta leaves the mass number unchanged.
The atomic number rises, not falls, in beta-minus.
Neither number falls in beta decay.

check.stem: Why can the daughter element’s name be skipped when balancing decay equations?

options.text: because the balanced atomic and mass numbers identify the nucleus completely
options.explanation: The two numbers plus the symbol pattern are what equations require.
Names are simply unnecessary for the marks.
Daughters vary with the parent.

options.text: because the daughter is always an isotope of the parent
options.explanation: Alpha and beta change the element.

check.stem: State the two balances that must hold in any nuclear decay equation.
check.modelAnswer: The total mass numbers before and after must be equal, and the total atomic numbers before and after must be equal.

check.stem: Write the decay equation in words for polonium-212 emitting an alpha particle.
check.modelAnswer: Polonium-212 decays to lead-208 with the emission of an alpha particle, balancing as 212 = 208 + 4 and 84 = 82 + 2.

check.stem: Explain why the atomic numbers must balance on either side of a decay equation.
check.modelAnswer: Charge is conserved in the decay: the bottom numbers count charge, so the charge carried by the parent must reappear as the daughter plus the emission.

check.stem: A nucleus contains 84 protons and 126 neutrons and alpha-decays to lead (symbol Pb). Give the daughter’s mass and atomic numbers.
check.modelAnswer: Parent mass = 84 + 126 = 210; daughter: atomic number 84 − 2 = 82, mass number 210 − 4 = 206.

glossary.definition: Emission of a helium nucleus, lowering the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.
Conversion of a neutron into a proton with emission of an electron; A unchanged, Z + 1.
Emission of a gamma ray that lowers the nucleus’s energy without changing either number.
Ejection of a neutron: mass number − 1, atomic number unchanged.

workedExample.prompt: A nucleus with 84 protons and 126 neutrons undergoes alpha decay and forms lead. Which isotope of lead forms?
steps: Alpha decay removes 2 protons: atomic number 84 − 2 = 82.
Alpha decay removes 4 nucleons: mass number 210 − 4 = 206.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The daughter is lead-206, with atomic number 82 and mass number 206.
